opus-5.5.text:
I think that claim mixes up two things: whether a particular simulator was good enough, and whether synthetic data *in principle* can carry real skills. People tried sim-to-real years ago, saw the gap, and concluded it doesn't work. But the gap isn't a law of nature. It's an engineering problem, and it's shrinking very fast.

Look at what's already happened. Locomotion is the clearest case. Almost every legged robot or humanoid you see walking, running, or recovering from a push today was trained mostly or entirely in simulation with reinforcement learning, then deployed zero-shot. Nobody seriously argues anymore that sim-trained locomotion can't transfer. So the question isn't "can it transfer," it's "which skills transfer, and what does it take."

For manipulation, especially grasping, our own work points the same way. We built very large synthetic datasets: millions of objects, billions of grasp poses, rendered under randomized lighting, materials, camera noise, and clutter. A model trained only on that data can pick up objects in the real world that it has never seen, at a high success rate. The key is that the policy is learning geometry and physical relationships, which are the parts simulation gets right, rather than memorizing the exact appearance of one lab's table. When you randomize enough, the real world just becomes another sample from the distribution.

There's also a practical argument. Real-world teleoperation data is extremely expensive and slow. You need people, robots, and hardware that breaks, and you get maybe thousands of hours. That's tiny compared to what large models need. If we insist that only real data counts, embodied AI will be stuck in a data-poor regime for a long time. Synthetic data is the only way I see to reach the scale of trillions of tokens, like language models have had.

I'm not saying real data is useless. The right recipe is to use synthetic data to build broad, general capabilities and a strong prior, then use a relatively small amount of real data to align and fine-tune, the way pretraining and post-training work in LLMs. But rejecting synthetic data outright because early simulators were crude is, to me, like rejecting neural networks in the 1990s because they didn't work yet. The evidence is already moving the other way.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation gets some geometry and physical relationships right and calls the gap an engineering problem, but it does not clearly distinguish approximate simulated physics from physics that is entirely different from real physics.

r002.rationale: It cites legged robots and humanoids trained mostly or entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot as evidence that sim-to-real transfer works.

r003.rationale: It describes models trained only on large synthetic rendered datasets picking up unseen objects in the real world, directly giving successful synthetic-to-real grasping as evidence.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss VLM pretraining on mixed real and synthetic visual media or connect that pretraining to visual transfer in VLA models.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the claim confuses a failure of method with a limit of principle. When people say synthetic data can't transfer, what they usually mean is that the sim-to-real work they've seen didn't transfer. And honestly, a lot of it didn't. But that was because the simulation was wrong in ways that mattered, not because simulation is wrong in principle.

Think about what a robot actually needs to learn for a skill like grasping or opening a drawer. It needs geometry, contact, how objects move when you push them. These are physical laws. They don't change between the simulated world and the real one. What changes is the rendering, the sensor noise, the friction coefficients, the small details of a particular object. And those are precisely the things you can randomize. If the policy has seen a hundred thousand drawers with different textures, handles, lighting, and dynamics, then the real drawer is just one more sample from that distribution. It's not a different world. It's a point inside the world the robot already trained on.

The second part of the argument is about data. Real robot data is expensive. One robot, one arm, one teleoperator, you get maybe a few hundred demonstrations a day, and every one of them is in the same lab with the same lighting. Simulation gives you millions of trajectories across thousands of scenes, and the cost of a failure is zero. No one breaks anything. So the question isn't synthetic versus real. It's whether you'd rather have a small amount of perfectly realistic data or a huge amount of slightly imperfect data that covers far more situations. For generalization, coverage wins.

And then there's the empirical point, which to me is the strongest. We've done this. We trained grasping and dexterous manipulation policies entirely in simulation, no real data at all, and deployed them on physical hands on objects they'd never seen. They worked. Not perfectly, not every time, but at rates that were competitive with or better than systems trained on real demonstrations. Once you've seen that happen, the claim that it "cannot" transfer just isn't a claim you can keep making. You have to retreat to something weaker, like "it's hard" or "it doesn't always transfer," and I'd agree with both of those.

So my position is actually quite moderate. Synthetic data isn't a replacement for everything. There are tasks, especially with deformable objects or fluids, where the simulators still aren't good enough, and real data helps close that last gap. But the direction is clear. Simulation is getting better every year, and real data collection isn't getting fundamentally cheaper. If you're building a robot that has to work in a kitchen it's never been in, you're going to need the scale that only synthetic data can give you.

r001.rationale: The response says the relevant physical laws do not change between simulated and real worlds, while simulation can be wrong in consequential details such as rendering, noise, and friction. This distinguishes approximation from an entirely different reality.

r003.rationale: It cites grasping policies trained entirely in simulation and deployed in the real world, but does not specify that they learned from synthetic visual data.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim is too absolute. A gap between simulation and reality doesn’t mean that nothing learned in simulation can transfer. The question is what the robot learns, and whether those things remain useful in the real world.

For example, synthetic data can vary lighting, textures, object shapes, and physical properties. That gives us a way to train a policy to handle variation rather than depend on one very specific environment. Of course, contact, friction, and sensing errors can still create problems, so transfer isn’t automatic.

But that’s a reason to test carefully and improve the simulation or adapt the policy—not a reason to rule out synthetic data. The meaningful test is whether the robot can perform the skill on real hardware under conditions it hasn’t seen before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that claim is too absolute. The question is whether the synthetic data captures the aspects of the task that matter in the real world. A simulator will never reproduce every detail, but a robot doesn’t necessarily need every detail to learn a useful skill.

For example, we can vary object shapes, lighting, friction, and other conditions during training so the policy doesn’t depend on one particular setup. There will still be a gap between simulation and reality, and some skills may require real-world adaptation. But that makes transfer a problem to measure and improve—not a reason to conclude that synthetic data cannot work.
